TO: The Honorable Joseph Rafferty The Honorable Kelly Noonan Murphy, Co-Chairs Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
DATE: April 3, 2025
RE: LD 783, An Act to Continue Support for the Maine Multicultural Center
Good afternoon Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and members of the committee-
My name is Aaliyah Merz. I'm a resident of Orono. I am here today as an Orono High School student on behalf of our Civil Rights Team. We are testifying in support of LD 783.
Under Maine's Attorney General and Department of Education, the Civil Rights Team is a student-based group working to create a safe and welcoming learning environment for students of all races, national origins, ancestries, genders, sexualities, religions, and abilities. Our work to protect students from all national origins and ancestries, specifically, is what brings us here today.
LD 783 will allocate money for the Maine Multicultural Center. In return, the money allocated will allow immigrant parents in our community to find employment using training they already have. In our school community, we have a good amount of families who are immigrants where parents have professional training from their home countries. For these families, having support to continue their careers in Maine could dramatically improve both their economic stability and their children's educational experience.
When people come here they shouldn't have to start from scratch or without a support system, but sadly, more often than not, that's what happens. The Maine Multi-Cultural Center provides resources for these immigrants that help them integrate into Maine society and provide things to help them get started and acclimate. These are things like: education--on the U.S. immigration system and language, support--to find accommodations and to help them feel at home, safe spaces--where families and individuals can connect, and, most importantly, training--so that they can enter the workforce. However, without proper funding for dedicated staff positions, the Center cannot effectively serve these skilled immigrants.  The MultiCultural Center's work directly supports our Civil Rights Team's goal of creating a welcoming environment for students of all national origins. In our school, we see firsthand how immigrant students can thrive when they and their families are supported. When people feel safe and welcomed, they become better students. If these students are simply placed in classrooms without guidance, they often struggle to find their place in the classroom and school.

When immigrant parents can find employment that matches their education and training, their children have more stability and better educational outcomes. This funding will help empower these families and enrich our entire community.
We urge the committee to vote in favor of LD 783. Thank you for considering our testimony.
10041497:
Written testimony in favor of LD 783 "An Act to Continue Support for the Maine Multicultural Center"
As a Banger Adult Education teacher of English for Speakers of Other Languages I have worked with students from many backgrounds from other countries for over 30 years. I saw them try to navigate transportation, medical appointments, housing needs, employment and paperwork all while speaking and reading with limited English.
I often tried to troubleshoot within the limited time frame I had with them while teaching English classes with multiple students while working 23 days a week.
Once the Maine Multicultural Center (MMCC) came upon the scene, my students had increased support to help them navigate daily life tasks facing an immigrant in the Bangor area. Now, they have a support team of volunteers to drive them to classes and appointments. MMCC volunteers and staff help them directly with paperwork for employment, housing forms grocery shopping, and government appointments (often in Portland). Volunteers help out with childcare as well.
I personally have served and continue to serve directly on a few different committees since 2018.
First,we have the Education Committee to reach out to the general public to better inform them of who we work with and how to better interact with a foreign-born population through teacher workshops,Community Forums, and small group cultural presentations.
Next, I work doing move-ins where we set up a home for new immigrant families. We rent storage space to collect household furnishings and a truck to deliver the furniture and houseware with volunteer movers who assemble furniture and clean the apartment before stocking the kitchen and bathroom.
Most importantly, I am part of a Support Team of 3 that assists a refugee family of 6. We took them to Walmart for food, clothes, and haircuts. We took them to the Mosque for worship services and to government offices for important meetings. We visited the post office to mail official forms. After living in a refugee camp for many years, they had to catch up on their shots, dental care, and medical care for serious ailments. During this time, they studied English and some of them worked or went to school full time. Gradually, they learned to drive in Maine, obtained a license and bought a van.

Without the help and support of MMCC this family would have missed many important deadlines and appointments. The bus runs close to their house, but it is cumbersome, especially for those with health issues.
I am happy to report that after 1 year in Maine, they are self-sufficient. Thanks to the support team accompaniment, they know their way around Bangor, support their son's soccer team and attend school and government meetings on time.
By supporting Maine MultiCultural Center, immigrant workers will be welcomed to Maine to help address labor shortages, start their own businesses and add to the culture of Maine. Legislative funding will keep our knowledgeable staff employed helping New Mainers.
Barbara Heal Miller April 1, 2025 Winterport, ME

10044455:
Education and Cultural Affairs Committee
Testimony in Support of LD 783 - An Act to Continue Support for the Maine Multicultural Center
April 14, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and Honorable Members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee, my name is Debbie Laurie and I am the City Manager for the City of Bangor. I am writing in support of LD 783, An Act to Continue Support for the Maine Multicultural Center.
The Maine Multicultural Center was founded, in part, to address a labor shortage in our region. The Maine Department of Labor has predicted a shortage of 90,000 workers over a decade as older Mainers retire and leave the workforce. Even if all the people born in Maine stayed and launched careers here, there still would not be enough new workers to replace those retiring. It became clear that we needed people to migrate to Maine if our economy was to continue to thrive, and that migration is happening. The center is currently working with approximately 200 immigrants, which include 13 single individuals and about 40 families.
The Committee last term passed a bill to provide state funding for the center, and that bill passed in both chambers. State Sen. Michael Tipping has noted that it allowed the center to fund the work of a program manager and two outreach coordinators, and also secure new private and federal funding. They have trained dozens of volunteers who are assigned to new families moving to our area. They assist them in getting jobs, finding housing, pursuing education, navigating a new culture and contributing to our state.
LD 783 would continue that funding for another two years and allow the center to continue its important work. The center has professionalized its operations, sought new sources of ongoing funding, connected with other local organizations to amplify its programs, and have made sure that new families continue to be welcomed and integrated in the Bangor area.
The City of Bangor has shown its commitment to supporting the center by previously directing $70,700 in ARPA funding to it. The Committee has the opportunity to approve state funding that will allow the center to recruit, train and sustain volunteers who will provide crucial support needed by immigrants to get started in their goal to have a safe and secure life for their families and be productive and contributing members of our Maine communities.
Thank you for your consideration, and please do not hesitate to reach out with any questions.
Debbie Laurie, City Manager, debbie.laurie@bangormaine.gov Cara Pelletier, City Council Chair, cara.pelletier@bangormaine.gov

10041793:
Nancy Jacobson Bangor LD 783
I am writing this testimony in support of the legislation to provide funding for the Maine Multicultural Center in Bangor. My name is Nancy Jacobson and I have been a resident of the Bangor area for 35 years and have worked with immigrants for 24 years as a teacher and as a volunteer. I have been a volunteer with MMCC for several years.
The importance of MMCC stems from both its unique role in supporting immigrants to the Bangor area as well as the importance of immigrants to our community, culturally and economically.
Catholic Charities of Maine created a Refugee Resettlement Area here in 2022. Since that time, MMCC has taken an important role in supporting over 200 refugees, asylum seekers and voluntary immigrants who have come to the area. CCM has a limited staff to help refugees in very important but specific ways when they first arrive in the area. MMCC staff and volunteers provide broad and ongoing assistance until the family is ready to be independent . The staff assists with legal and business paperwork, helps register both children and adults for school and training programs, connects immigrants to services and resources in the community, furnishes homes for the newly arrived immigrants, and recruits, trains and supports volunteers. MMCC volunteers help with attending appointments, shopping, transportation, learning about the area, learning English, learning to drive, and generally helping the new arrivals integrate.
MMCC is the only organization to help asylum seekers, who have even more diverse and complex needs and have many fewer of the supports that refugees have. Meanwhile, many of the voluntary immigrants come with jobs but need help finding their way to resources, integrating into the community and so appreciate the welcoming that MMCC volunteers provide.
Above are the supports that MMCC provides to immigrants. At the same time, newcomers support our community in important ways economically. We know that Maine has a declining population and in the Bangor area we have had difficulty filling needed workers both for simple and skilled labor. Immigrants provide both and research shows that a higher percentage of immigrants go on to open their own businesses than native-born Americans. Immigrants also help maintain the population in our communities and schools.
Then there are the cultural benefits to our community from incorporating immigrants. Americans often say we are a country of immigrants. How better for us to appreciate our roots and teach our children about those roots than to welcome immigrants who are eager to improve their lives, who show us a can-do and brave approach, who need our help and teach us about being compassionate, and who are ready to share with us about their home country's language, food, culture, politics, religion and more. How better to broaden our own lives? I speak as a teacher and parent when I say that having these children and families in our schools and communities enriches our lives through experiences that we could only previously imagine from Maine.

This Bill will ensure that the Maine Multicultural Center's vital work continues. MMCC is good for Maine, and our work is good for local communities.
The Maine Multicultural Center was formed partly to address the state's worker crisis. Maine's workforce is aging rapidly, with many retiring and not enough people to replace them. The State's Department of Labor estimated that Maine will need 90,000 new workers during this decade to address its shortfall, an equivalent of 9,000 per year. Maine cannot achieve this goal without immigrants.
Since its inception, the Maine Multicultural Center has worked to further Maine's interests. MMCC provides service to the community in three general categories:
 Refugees are legal migrants resettled in the United States. Through the Refugee Resettlement Program led by Catholic Charities, the MMCC provides a link by helping families navigate the complex dynamics of living in a new country. For example, families arriving from war-torn countries have no more than the clothes on their backs. MMCC solicits donations of clothes and furniture, coordinates volunteers to assist with movein, and helps the families assimilate to Maine's culture.
 Asylum Seekers are immigrants seeking protection from violence, including gangs, political persecution, and other threats with dire consequences. Like refugees, they have little to nothing. These individuals often seek refuge in democracy. They value freedom and believe in the American dream. Similarly, the MMCC coordinates efforts to help asylees with legal status integrate into the community.
 Voluntary Migrants arrive in the U.S. with work visas and permits and are legally authorized to work. Many volunteer migrants fill positions that Americans have abandoned for better working conditions and pay. The Maine Multicultural Center helps volunteer migrants integrate and provides support as needed.

The immigrant population in Maine has an essential role in filling critical jobs in the state and adding to the rich traditions that Mainers embrace. As the saying goes, "If you want to be a Mainer, welcome to Maine." An overwhelming majority of immigrants who arrive in Maine come from countries ravaged by war or have fled violence in pursuit of better opportunities in a democratic country. They are happy to integrate into the community and content to call themselves Mainers. Immigrants contribute exponentially to Maine economically, culturally, and socially. According to the report "Starting Anew: The Economic Impact of Refugees in America," there is compelling evidence that refugees have become an indispensable part of their local communities, revitalizing cities and towns nationwide. Decades of data show that refugees and asylees make significant contributions to and strengthen the U.S. economy, generating a net fiscal benefit of $123.8 billion to the U.S. government from 2005 to 2019.
LD 783 will allow the MMCC to continue funding two positions vital to meeting Maine's workforce needs. We ask for your support of LD 783 with profound gratitude as we continue to do the work that moves Maine forward.

Tom Armstrong Bangor LD 783
My name is Thomas Armstrong. I live at 61 Madison Street in Bangor. Over a year ago, my wife Barbara and I became volunteers with the Maine Multi Cultural Center. We know first hand how immigrants bring strengths to Maine. They have skills to fill jobs we need filled, and the initiative to work hard and succeed. The family we work with has a young father, mother, and five children. The father soon found work here as a carpenter. The mom has a young one, under 3, and four other school age children. All are making great strides in learning English. They call the USA "Paradise" compared to the places they had lived in as refugees. We as volunteers have aided them with transportation to medical appointments and English lessons, helped with setting up bank accounts, attended school meetings and functions with them. We have become their friends, providing information and support as needed. We are always impressed with their bravery and determination to become part of the Bangor community. MMCC staff provides the guidance and systematic information volunteers need to properly help the families integrate into life in the USA. Although we as volunteers are willing and eager to assist the family to which we were assigned, without the staff guidance and training, we would not have known what was needed, and how to provide assistance to the family. We encourage you to provide funding to Maine Multi Cultural Center to continue their work with refuge families so these families can become fully contributing members of our American society.
